summary_findings: THE OCCUPATIONAL AND CASTE AXIS IS ALMOST UNRECORDED, AND THAT IS THIS WAVE'S RESULT. The plan aimed at sky-names keyed to what people do rather than to what they speak — pastoralists (Dhangar, Kuruba, Gujjar, Rabari, Bharvad, Golla), fishing castes, the Banjara outside Vidarbha. Three of the largest folklore compendia of colonial India were downloaded in full and cross-searched: Enthoven's Folklore of Bombay (1924) and both volumes of Crooke's Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India (1896), every line containing a sky word tested against twenty occupational and caste terms. THE CROSS-SEARCH RETURNED ONE HIT IN THREE VOLUMES, and it was a false positive. This is the same shape the database has met four times already: Russell and Hiralal yielded one community with named figures in four volumes (the Dhuri), Thurston almost nothing in seven, Rose's Glossary nothing in the volume obtained. The colonial compendia record sky-lore by LANGUAGE and by TRIBE, and essentially never by trade. WHAT THE COMPENDIA DO HAVE HAD MOSTLY BEEN TAKEN ALREADY. Enthoven's chapter on stars and planets was worked in an earlier pass and eight entries in marathi_gujarati.json come from it, including the two best occupational items in the whole database: GADLI, Rohiṇī and Kṛttikā together, 'supposed to indicate the rise and fall in the cotton-market' — the only commodity omen here — and the Konkan death-divination in which a man who cannot make out the pole star, or in the other version Arundhatī, has six months to live. Re-reading the chapter yielded three things it had missed, entered here. FIRST, THE FOUR MAṆḌALAS. A meteor is read by which quarter of the sky it falls from: Vāyu-maṇḍal portends an epidemic, Varuṇa-maṇḍal is favourable to human happiness, Indra-maṇḍal threatens kings, Agni-maṇḍal threatens war between nations. This is a partition of the sky the database did not have — the Sanskrit compilation carries the nine vīthīs, the planets' roads, and Rajasthani keeps one of them, but the maṇḍalas divide by presiding deity and exist only to answer where a meteor came from. And in the same passage is the sharpest occupational split recorded anywhere here: a meteor falling into the sea forebodes evil to the dwellers on earth generally, but IN THE KANARA DISTRICT the same fall is held to promise rain. A coast that wants rain reads the omen the other way up. SECOND, TĀRĀ-BĀRAS, the name of the rite of showing the pole star to a couple as soon as the marriage knot is tied — the only name for a sky-RITE in this database, everything else here naming a star, a figure, a wind or a season. THIRD, CROOKE ON MŪLA, which corroborates a Wave 4 finding from nine hundred kilometres away and thirty-five years earlier. Turner's Nepali dictionary has मुल्याहा mulyāhā, 'born under mul', meaning as a noun 'an unfortunate person, an orphan'. Crooke gives the social fact behind the word: the twenty-seven asterisms serve only to cast a marriage horoscope, and the one an ordinary cultivator must reckon with is the unlucky Mūla, because a son born under it needs an elaborate purification. An asterism that matters as a social category rather than as a season or a shape. THE SCHEMA CHANGED HERE, WHICH IS WHAT THIS WAVE WAS REALLY FOR. The expansion plan flagged from the start that this database is keyed on language while the question being asked is partly about communities, and that the mismatch had already bitten once — the Chhattisgarhi Dhuri entries in tribal.json had to be argued into a caveat because the Dhuri are a caste and not a language. An optional `community` field is now part of the schema, carried by the three entries in this file and back-filled onto the five earlier entries that had a community buried in their `region` string: the Dhuri rice-parchers of Chhattisgarh, the Deshasth Brahmans of Dharwar, the Konda Dora of the Vizagapatam Agency, the Uppu Yerukala or Korava of the Telugu country, and the Lingāyat cultivators of Bellary whose kārte rain-calendar Thurston recorded. Eight entries out of 777 carry a community, and that ratio is the finding restated.

entries.sky_object: the four maṇḍalas — quarters of the sky by presiding deity, by which the fall of a meteor is read

modern_star.common_name: four named divisions of the sky, unlocated by the source

entries.community: Konkan and Deccan Hindu households; Enthoven's informants are not further specified
entries.literal_meaning: 'the circle of Vāyu (wind), of Varuṇa (waters), of Indra, of Agni (fire)'
entries.usage_note: A meteor is auspicious or baneful according to which group it is seen to fall from: out of the Vāyu-maṇḍal it portends an epidemic; out of the Varuṇa-maṇḍal it is favourable to human happiness; out of the Indra-maṇḍal it forebodes danger to all kings; out of the Agni-maṇḍal it threatens war between nations. Enthoven adds that during the monsoon the rain is expected in whatever direction a meteor shoots, and that in the Kanara District a meteor falling into the sea is held to promise rain — the same event read as a threat inland and as a blessing on the coast.
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 71
entries.quote: Some persons, however, regard the appearance of meteors as auspicious or baneful, according to the group of stars from which they are seen to fall. Meteors from the Vayu-mandal (or the groups of stars known by the name of Vayu), portend the breaking out of an epidemic : those from Varuna-mandal are believed to be favourable to human happiness : if they fall from Indra-mandal, they forebode danger to all kings ; those from Agni-mandal threaten war between nations.
entries.notes: A DIVISION OF THE SKY THIS DATABASE DID NOT HAVE. The Sanskrit compilation carries the nine vīthīs, the star-roads, and Rajasthani keeps them (gajabīthī in hindi_urdu_punjabi.json); the maṇḍalas are a different partition, by presiding deity rather than by the planets' path, and they exist here only to answer where a meteor came from. Enthoven does not say which stars belong to which maṇḍal and no attempt is made here to supply them — hence `likely` and a modern_star that says so. The Kanara reading in the usage note is the clearest occupational split in this file: the same meteor is a portent of evil to the dwellers on earth generally and a promise of rain to a coastal district that wants rain.

entries.sky_object: the pole star, in the rite of showing it to a newly married couple
entries.community: Konkan and Deccan Hindu families of the higher castes
entries.literal_meaning: 'the star twelfth', bāras being the twelfth day of the lunar fortnight
entries.usage_note: Married couples are made to look at the pole star immediately after the priest ties the marriage knot; Enthoven names the rite in a footnote. The showing of Arundhatī to the bride, as a lesson in chastity, is the companion rite on the same page.
entries.citation: R. E. Enthoven, The Folklore of Bombay (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924), p. 68
entries.quote: Married couples are made to look at the pole-star immediately after the marriage knot is tied by the priest, in the hope … This is known as Tara-baras.
entries.notes: The only NAME FOR A SKY-RITE in this database — everything else here names a star, a figure, a wind or a season. Enthoven's footnote marker sits at the end of a sentence that the archive.org scan breaks mid-clause, so the quote is given with an ellipsis where the page is unreadable, and the entry is graded `likely` on that account rather than on any doubt about the rite. Compare the Telugu and Assamese Arundhatī entries already in this database, which are the same wedding ritual seen from two other languages, and the caveat there about what a `borrowed` tag does and does not claim about the people performing it.

entries.sky_object: Mūla, the nineteenth nakshatra, and being born under it
entries.region: the North-Western Provinces and Oudh (Upper India)
entries.usage_note: Crooke's point is a social one: the twenty-seven asterisms are used only in calculating the marriage horoscope, and the one an ordinary cultivator actually has to reckon with is the unlucky Mūla — a son born under it must undergo an elaborate purification.
entries.citation: William Crooke, The Popular Religion and Folk-lore of Northern India, 2nd ed. (Westminster: Archibald Constable, 1896), vol. I, p. 24
entries.quote: These are used only in calculating the marriage horoscope, and the only one of them with which the fairly well-to-do rustic has much concern is with the unlucky Mula. Should by an evil chance his son be born in this asterism, he has to undergo a most elaborate rite of purification.
entries.notes: CORROBORATES THE NEPALI FINDING OF WAVE 4 FROM 900 KM AWAY AND 35 YEARS EARLIER. Turner's Nepali dictionary derives मुल्याहा mulyāhā, 'born under mul', which as a noun means 'an unfortunate person, an orphan' (himalaya.json). Crooke, without a dictionary, gives the social fact behind it: of twenty-seven asterisms this is the one that reaches a farming household, and it reaches it by marking a child. Together the two are the database's clearest case of an asterism that matters as a social category rather than as a season or a shape.

caveats: Both sources are public domain and are quoted verbatim from the archive.org full text: Enthoven died in 1952 and Crooke in 1923. The scans are clean enough to quote except at one point, noted in the Tārā-bāras entry, where a sentence breaks mid-clause across a footnote marker and the quote carries an ellipsis.

THE NEGATIVE IS THE MAIN RESULT AND ITS METHOD SHOULD BE STATED. Every line of the three volumes containing any of star, stars, constellation, Pleiades, Orion, Great Bear, Milky Way, galaxy, comet, Saptarshi, Arundhati, Krittika or Rohini was extracted with four lines of context either side and tested against Dhangar, Koli, Kunbi, Rabari, Gujjar, Bharvad, Ahir, Gowli, Golla, Kuruba, Idaiyar, fisher, shepherd, herdsman, cowherd, Bhandari, Agri, Mahar, Ramoshi and Vanjari. One line matched, and it matched on the word 'shepherd' inside an unrelated phrase. That is a fact about what colonial folklorists collected, not a claim that pastoralists and fishermen have no sky.

The four maṇḍalas are graded `likely` and their `modern_star` says in words that the source does not locate them. Enthoven names the divisions and their omens and never says which stars belong to which; the obvious guess — that they are the directional quarters of the classical dikpāla scheme — is a guess, and this database does not force identifications.

Tārā-bāras is graded `likely` for a textual reason and not a substantive one: Enthoven gives the name only in a footnote, and the sentence it is attached to is broken in the scan. The rite itself is not in doubt and is corroborated by the Telugu and Assamese Arundhatī entries already in the database, which record the companion showing of Arundhatī to the bride.

The new `community` field is OPTIONAL and most entries will never carry one. It records the caste, occupational group or ethnonym a source names, in the source's own words, and it is not a claim that the name belongs only to that group — Enthoven's 'Konkan and Deccan Hindu families of the higher castes' is his phrase and his social framing, reproduced rather than endorsed. Where a source names no community the field is absent, which is the honest default and is true of 769 of the 777 entries.

Back-filling the field changed five entries in three earlier files and changed nothing else about them: the community was already stated inside their `region` string and has been lifted out, not invented. The region strings were left as they stand so that nothing is lost if the new field is ever dropped.
